History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
26-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presents with a 3-day progressively worsening right-predominant, photophobic headache unresponsive to low-dose ibuprofen; clinical impression is most consistent with an acute migraine episode.

History:
• Presenting complaint: “Crazy headache” for 3 days.  
• Timeline/Progression:  
  – Day 0: Gradual onset at work; worsened by end of day.  
  – Day 1-3: Persistently present; intensity ≥8/10; further worsening despite sleep.  
• Character: Dull constant ache with intermittent sharper spikes; maximal around right eye but “all over” head.  
• Severity: 8/10.  
• Aggravating factors: Bright light (photophobia); computer screen; stress (minor).  
• Relieving/attempted: Tried ibuprofen “three a day” for 2 days—no relief; reduced screen brightness; sleep ineffective.  
• Associated symptoms: Photophobia (“light hurts”); brief “shooting lights” at onset; nausea (no vomiting); difficulty concentrating.  
• Pertinent negatives: No blurred vision, vision loss, neck stiffness, speech difficulty, limb weakness, fever, rash, recent head trauma.  
• Review of systems (only items discussed):  
  – Constitutional: No fever.  
  – HEENT: Photophobia; no sinus congestion reported.  
  – Neuro: Headache as above; no focal deficits.  
  – GI: Nausea without vomiting.  
  – Skin: No rash.  

Past Medical History:
• No chronic illnesses reported.  
• No prior personal history of migraine; previous episodic headaches resolved with NSAIDs.  
Medications: None regular. Ibuprofen self-administered (3 tablets/day, dose/route/frequency otherwise not documented).  
Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Lives with three housemates.  
• Occupation: IT professional (heavy computer use).  
• Smoking: Social smoker.  
• Alcohol: Social drinker.  
• Drugs: None mentioned.  
• Stress: Mild work stress (new project).  
• Vision: Wears glasses since age 5; no recent eye exam.

Family History:
• Mother and sister with recurrent migraines (mother more severe, season-triggered).

Physical Examination:
(No in-person exam; tele-consult)  
• Vitals: Not obtained.  
• General/Neuro/HEENT: Not examined.

Investigations:
• None performed or available.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Acute severe headache, likely migraine (first episode):  
  • Assessment: Meets migraine features—unilateral predominance, photophobia, visual aura-like phenomena, nausea, strong family history. Tension-type headache less likely; no red-flag features for intracranial pathology currently.  
  • Plan:  
    – Optimize NSAID dosing: Up to ibuprofen 400 mg two tablets three times daily with food (patient education).  
    – Offer prescription for stronger NSAID (Naproxen) and consider adding acetaminophen or codeine as rescue analgesia (per discussion).  
    – Initiate headache diary to document frequency, triggers, response to medications.  
    – Provide written/worsening advice: Return immediately for visual changes, focal weakness, escalating pain, vomiting, or other concerning symptoms.  
    – Follow-up: Re-evaluation in 1–2 weeks; consider prophylactic therapy if headaches become recurrent.  

Issue 2 – Photophobia / possible eye-strain contribution:  
  • Assessment: Bright-light sensitivity may be part of migraine; prolonged screen use and outdated prescription could exacerbate.  
  • Plan: Recommend scheduling formal eye examination; continue reduced screen brightness and regular breaks.

Issue 3 – Lifestyle factors:  
  • Assessment: Social smoking and mild work stress may act as headache triggers.  
  • Plan: Brief counselling given on potential benefit of smoking reduction/cessation and stress-management; further discussion at follow-up.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Migraine with possible aura – High likelihood: Right-sided pain, photophobia, visual scintillations, nausea, strong family history, typical demographic.  
2. Tension-type headache – Moderate likelihood: Diffuse dull pain and work stress, but photophobia and visual aura less characteristic.  
3. Acute frontal/ethmoid sinusitis – Low likelihood: Periorbital pain and gradual course, but lacks congestion, fever, or facial tenderness.

Quality checks:

• Missing but expected: Objective vitals, focused neurological and fundoscopic examination, medication dose/route/frequency details, allergy confirmation, contraceptive use clarification.  
• Transcript/DDx conflicts: None noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear with minimal filler; no inaudible sections.
